newsitem.title: UK: Bond markets see no big scares in U.S. election.
newsitem.headline: Bond markets see no big scares in U.S. election.

text.p: Bond markets are watching the U.S. election with calm bordering on apathy, and even the idea of large Democrat gains -- historically considered bearish for markets -- is seen as no cause for panic.

"If one or both houses of Congress went Democrat, there might be a temporary kneejerk reaction that was negative for Treasuries, but I imagine that would be the time to start buying them," said Lee Ferridge at NatWest Capital Markets.

"I don't see any scary outcomes for bonds," said Ferridge, a currency strategist. "There is political will to reduce government deficits not only in the U.S. but elsewhere -- and that goes for Democrats and Republicans."

President Bill Clinton is so far ahead in opinion polls that markets almost take it for granted he will be re-elected on November 5, and attention has turned to the political complexion of the legislature he would govern with next year.

Both the House of Representatives and the Senate are at present controlled by the Republicans, who are traditionally more trusted than Democrats to shun the high-spending ways that make bond markets skittish.
But analysts said traditional stereotypes have been stood on their head by Clinton's drive to curtail the budget deficit and by the high-spending of preceding Republican administrations.

"It might be slightly negative for markets due to historical perceptions (if the Democrats make big gains in the legislature) but don't expect major fallout," said Brian Venables, senior bond strategist at ABN-AMRO Hoare Govett in Amsterdam.
Governments fund their public deficits by issuing bonds and markets therefore are always on guard for any signs of extra debt supply as a result of fiscal problems.

Venables drew a distinction between a clean sweep of Capitol Hill by the Democrats, which would prompt market fears of a reversion to old spendthrift ways, and the likelier event of only the House of Representatives changing hands.

"Probably the ideal would be to have one house become Democrat-controlled as it would give Clinton a greater mandate to be more decisive on policy -- which markets like. At the same time, the other house would act as a brake on power," he said.

A London-based economist said investors who were convinced there would be Democrat Congressional gains should consider going short of U.S. Treasuries into the elections and buying them back immediately afterwards.
The economist stressed that any setback for Treasuries would be temporary, and the market was likely to feel reassured after the new legislature had been in place for a month or two.
"Clinton wants to go down in history as the man who balanced the budget so a Democrat Congress might end up more sympathetic to his aims," said the economist.

Ferridge said Clinton would veto any "silly spending plans" by a new Democrat majority and tipped a strong Treasury rally could come early next year if markets judged Clinton was sticking to the deficit-cutting road.
He said this would reduce the yield spread of Treasuries over German Bunds from its current 70 basis points, but European markets would also be carried higher in the process.
Another bulwark against fiscal imprudence would be the Federal Reserve which Venables said would ratchet up interest rates if necessary to deter such behaviour.
Only in this hypothetical situation did he see risk of severe damage to U.S. bonds, with an accompanying danger of economic slowdown.

The immediate transatlantic impact in that case would be on British gilts, as Britain is more closely aligned with U.S. economic cycles. But the longer term harm would be to countries aspiring to membership of the European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), Venables added.
He said France and Germany would be most vulnerable in this connection as they needed healthy U.S. export markets to get the growth required to meet the EMU Maastricht treaty criteria.
Analysts said apathetic markets had not focused much on what would happen if Republican underdog Bob Dole won the presidency.
Ferridge said bonds could be unsettled if Clinton's big opinion poll lead fell greatly in the final runup to November 5, but this was simply because the market did not like uncertainty.
Dole's pledge for 15 percent income tax cuts would not faze the bond market so long as it was matched by savings and did not send up the deficit, he said.
